column8: In March 1815 Napoleon escaped from exile on Elba and took back the throne of France. Europe's leading powers declared him an outlaw and prepared to fight him. Wellington commanded British, Dutch, Belgian and German troops across western Belgium, while Bloocher's Prussian corps were spread farther east, from Shar-luh-rwah toward Nah-moor and Lee-ezh. Napoleon decided to strike before the rest of the allies could join them.

At dawn on 15 June Napoleon's army, about 120,000 strong, advanced toward the Sahm-bruh. French troops crossed the river at several points, taking Shar-luh-rwah later that morning. Napoleon aimed his blow at the point where the two allied armies met, to drive between them and beat each one alone. The Prussian outposts fell back fighting toward Fluh-roos.

That evening many senior officers and members of Brussels society attended a ball given by the Duchess of Richmond. Wellington already knew the French had advanced. During the ball he received more news. One later account says he admitted Napoleon had surprised him and gained a day's march. As the night went on, officers left the ball to prepare their men and join the troops marching south.

On the 16th Napoleon attacked about eighty thousand Prussians from three corps, gathered around Leenyee and Saint- Amand. All afternoon the two armies fought for the villages, house by house. In the evening Napoleon sent in the Imperial Guard, and the Prussian centre broke.

At the same time, roughly eleven kilometres away in a straight line, Marshal Nay attacked the crossroads of Kat-ruh Brah. It was first defended by Dutch-Belgian troops under General Per-pon-shay. Wellington arrived in the morning, before Nay's main attack began, and all afternoon his regiments came up the road from Brussels and were thrown into the fight. By nightfall Nay had been held, and the crossroads was still in allied hands.

Between the battles, dairlon's corps of about twenty thousand men was redirected toward Leenyee, then recalled by Nay. It marched between the two battlefields and fought at neither. Its absence may have cost the French a greater victory at Leenyee, or success at Kat-ruh Brah. Historians still debate what its arrival might have changed.

At Leenyee, the seventy-two-year-old Bloocher led a last cavalry charge. His horse was shot and fell on him. French cavalry passed close by, but his aide Count Noss-tits stayed with him until Prussian soldiers could free him. While Bloocher was missing, his chief of staff Gny-zuh-now directed the defeated troops first toward Tee-yee, then toward Wahvruh, keeping them within reach of Wellington.

Retreating north to Wahvruh, not east toward their homeland, kept the two allied armies within supporting distance, and made their cooperation at Waterloo possible. Napoleon sent Marshal Grooshee with roughly thirty-three thousand men to pursue the Prussians, attack them if possible, and prevent them from joining Wellington. Grooshee's pursuit went slowly, by way of Zhahm-bloo, where he spent the night.

After learning that Bloocher had retreated from Leenyee, Wellington withdrew from Kat-ruh Brah, his left flank exposed, and marched north toward the ridge of Mon San Zhon. French cavalry pursued his rearguard and clashed with British cavalry near Zhuh-nap. A violent thunderstorm swept over the retreat, turning the roads and fields into mud.

All night the rain fell on two armies lying in the open fields, a few kilometres apart. Wellington prepared to fight on the ridge, provided Bloocher came to his aid from Wahvruh, and during the night the Prussians confirmed their promise to march. At dawn, Boolow's Prussian corps began moving west from Wahvruh along muddy roads, marching to Wellington's aid before the battle had begun.

On the morning of 18 June, Napoleon delayed his attack while his army assembled and the rain-soaked ground began to dry. Near Wahl-an, Grooshee heard the guns of Waterloo. General Zhay-rar urged him to march toward the fighting, but Grooshee refused and continued pursuing the Prussians toward Wahvruh. The battle of Waterloo had begun.
